text:
Abraham is commanded to take his son, his only son, whom he loves; and of what Abraham felt upon hearing it the narrator gives no account whatever. We are never admitted into his mind. He makes no protest; he does not bargain; there is nothing here of the man who pleaded so stubbornly with God for Sodom. What is left to us in his place is less a character than a silence, and in that silence, I think, lies the whole meaning of the episode. A question is put to the reader in this chapter, and it is never answered.

The three days of travel may be read as a kind of suspended sentence. Outwardly nothing happens in them; inwardly everything does. The writer lingers on the servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire, and by lingering on them he names the instruments of the act before he names the act itself. Obedience and horror are kept side by side through the whole journey, and neither is ever suffered to prevail over the other. Faith, as it appears in this story, has no warmth of feeling in it; it is a geometry, all lines and distances.

Isaac is the child of the covenant, the one through whom the nations are to be blessed; and it is this very promise that is now turned into a test. When we place the command beside the earlier promise, the distance between them grows less than we had supposed. Everything in the scene turns upon a single word, _hineni_, "here I am," which Abraham speaks three times: to God, to Isaac, and to the angel. Each time the word means something different. Each time it costs him more. For Abraham, to declare that he is present is to declare what he stands to lose.

What does Isaac know? We are not told. He carries the wood; he asks about the lamb; he receives an answer which is no answer at all. Of his thoughts the narrator offers nothing, only a verb: they went, both of them, together. The phrase recurs, as if repetition could stand in for explanation. Obedience, reckoned strictly, leaves nothing over and nothing unaccounted for; and the narrator, having raised the question of Isaac's consent, quietly sets it down.

He who would read this passage well must attend to what is left out of it, for much of its meaning lies there. Sarah is absent from the chapter entirely, and her death is announced in the very next verse. Without ever saying so, the writer lets us feel that something in the household did not survive the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants; Isaac is not mentioned. At the precise moment when a lesser story would linger, this one turns away. A silence of this kind is itself a sort of testimony, and it is Sarah, who never once appears, who bears the heaviest part of it.

It may be objected that the chapter merely follows the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains; and in some sense this is true. Yet the same narrator elsewhere tells us plainly what his people feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence here is deliberate. It was chosen, and it was not an accident of the manner. Restraint, in this writer, becomes a kind of accusation, and it is the more pointed because the pen that is silent over Abraham is the same that told us Joseph wept.

Between the God who promises and the God who demands, the writer makes no settlement; he keeps both before us and will not choose. Abraham stands on the mountain with the knife raised and the ram not yet seen, and there the reader is left with him. The question put to us admits of no answer, and its want of an answer is itself the answer we receive. Whoever reads the chapter is tried by it, as Abraham was.

Genesis 22 is, I believe, less a story about sacrifice than a story about reading; it teaches that the things of most importance are the things a writer declines to say. Abraham is silent; Isaac asks his question; Sarah is absent; the narrator will not explain. Each of these is a gap, and each gap makes its demand upon us; the very brevity of the telling lays the burden on the reader. What the writer withholds is what he gives, and nowhere more plainly than in the three words Abraham speaks upon the mountain, "here I am."
